title: What Are You Carrying?
opening: Maybe the question is not how much more we need. Maybe it is how much we are carrying that God never asked us to carry.
body:
Proverbs today contains a prayer that seems almost contrary to the way we are taught to live:

“Give me neither poverty nor riches; provide me only with the food I need.”

Only what I need.

There is something incredibly simple about that, and something incredibly difficult.

The writer understands the danger on both sides. Give me too much, and perhaps I become so comfortable that I begin to believe I no longer need God. Give me too little, and desperation may lead me to take what isn't mine and dishonor Him.

So he asks for neither.

He asks for enough.

It made me think about how early this struggle begins in us. A baby is hungry and cries. The need is met, the belly becomes full, and the crying stops. Then we become toddlers and discover another word: mine. We don't want to share. We want what someone else has. We want more.

Those basic needs don't disappear as we grow older. They become more complicated.

Food becomes possessions. Possessions become security. Security becomes success. Success becomes recognition. We begin adding things we believe we need in order to feel safe, important, comfortable or complete.

And somewhere along the way, “enough” becomes very difficult to recognize.

Then I read Luke.

Jesus sends the Twelve out to proclaim the Kingdom of God, giving them power and authority over demons and diseases. This is an enormous mission.

And then He tells them what to bring.

Almost nothing.

No walking stick. No sack. No food. No money. Not even a second tunic.

That stopped me.

If I were preparing for something important, my instinct would probably be the opposite. I would prepare for every possibility. Bring extra. Make sure there was enough money. Have another set of clothes. Know where I was staying. Have a backup plan.

Jesus sends them without those securities.

They will have to depend upon God.

They will have to depend upon the hospitality of others.

And some of those people will reject them.

Jesus tells them what to do then too.

Leave.

Shake the dust from your feet.

And keep going.

I realized how much I identify with that dust.

Lately I feel as though I am constantly shaking dust from my feet.

Disappointments. People. Expectations. Things that didn't turn out the way I thought they would. Situations that hurt. Moments when I believed I was doing the right thing and somehow still found myself wounded.

I shake the dust off.

But here is where I struggle.

Instead of continuing to the next village, sometimes I retreat.

I protect myself. I become cautious. I pull inward. I tell myself I have moved on, while somewhere inside I am still carrying what happened.

And maybe that isn't really shaking off the dust at all.

Maybe I have simply put it in my sack.

I carry the conversation.

I carry the resentment.

I carry what I wish I had said.

I carry the need to prove that I was right.

I carry the disappointment that someone wasn't who I thought they were.

I carry the fear that the next person might do the same thing.

Eventually, that becomes a very heavy sack.

And Jesus never told the disciples to carry it.

There is a difference between leaving something behind and closing yourself off because of it.

Jesus does not tell the Twelve to remain where they are rejected. That matters to me. Following Christ does not mean that we have to remain indefinitely in every place that wounds us.

But He also doesn't tell them to let one village end the mission.

Shake off the dust.

Keep walking.

Suddenly Proverbs feels connected to this in a way I didn't see at first.

“Provide me only with the food I need.”

Maybe that prayer is about more than possessions.

Maybe there are things inside me that I have accumulated too.

Resentment I don't need.

Fear I don't need.

Old arguments I don't need.

The need to be understood by everyone.

The need to prove myself.

The need to control what happens next.

The need to protect myself so completely that eventually no one can hurt me because no one can really reach me.

I say that I want Jesus in my heart. I want His love there. I want to see joy. I want to give light. I want my life to proclaim the Good News in whatever small way I can.

But the truth is that my heart gets crowded.

Some of it is filled with the wants and desires of this world.

And some of it is filled with dust from villages I already left.

Maybe God is asking me the same question today that Proverbs places before us:

What is enough?

Perhaps enough is not having every possible protection against tomorrow.

Perhaps enough is not having everyone understand me.

Perhaps enough is not finally winning every argument or correcting every wrong.

Perhaps enough is trusting that God will provide what is necessary for the next part of the journey.

And perhaps faith requires enough emptiness in our hands to receive it.

I don't think shaking the dust from our feet means becoming indifferent to what happened. Some things hurt. Some things require boundaries. Some things should be left.

But they do not have to become our permanent luggage.

That may be the part I need to learn.

I can leave the village without carrying the village with me.

I can be hurt without becoming hardened.

I can be rejected without retreating from everyone.

I can discover that something wasn't meant for me and still continue toward whatever God has placed ahead.

I don't have to carry enough for the entire journey today.

Maybe I only need enough for today.

His Word.

His grace.

His love.

And enough trust to take another step.

There are still villages ahead.

There are still people who need the Good News.

There is still light to give.

So perhaps when I feel myself retreating, I need to look down at what I am carrying and ask:

Did God actually ask me to bring this?

If not, perhaps it is time to put it down.

Shake off the dust.

And keep walking.
prayer: Lord, show me what I am carrying that You never asked me to carry. Teach me to recognize what is enough and to trust You for what I truly need. When I am hurt or rejected, give me the wisdom to know when to leave, but do not let disappointment harden my heart or stop the mission You have given me. Help me release resentment, fear, comparison, the need to control, and the need to be understood. Empty my hands of what belongs to yesterday so they are free to receive Your grace today. When I want to retreat, remind me that there are still villages ahead. Give me the courage to shake off the dust and keep walking with You. Amen.
theme: Trusting God for enough, letting go of excess and past hurts, rejection, spiritual dependence, and continuing forward in faith

body:
Today was hard.

My husband and I are suffering. There really isn't a prettier way to say it.

This past year has changed almost everything. An accident changed my health and eventually my work. I lost a career that had been part of my identity for years, along with the income, benefits, security, and sense of purpose that came with it. My husband underwent a complicated neck surgery that carried frightening possibilities. We bought a small business hoping to build something good together, only to discover that taking over someone else's business can also mean inheriting wounds, distrust, anger, and problems you did not create.

And lately it feels as though we keep trying to do the right thing while discovering one more difficult thing after another.

Today we were angry.

Angry about money. Angry about decisions we made when life was already upside down. Angry about people and situations we cannot change. Angry about things that seem unfair. Angry with ourselves for not knowing then what we know now.

And somewhere underneath all of that anger is exhaustion.

I keep trying to do what is right.

But sometimes doing what is right doesn't seem to make anything easier.

Then my husband read something to me about Mother Teresa and the spiritual darkness she experienced. I found myself almost stunned by it. Here was a woman whose life became synonymous with serving God through the poorest and most forgotten people, and yet she knew profound interior darkness.

How could someone who did so much good feel so tormented?

And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is: Why do I expect faith to protect me from feeling that way?

I think somewhere inside me I have believed that the closer I become to God, the happier I should become. That prayer should bring peace. Faith should bring certainty. Doing what is right should somehow make the road straighter.

Yet lately it seems that the more I know, the more I see.

I see suffering differently.

I see my own faults more clearly.

I see how easily anger enters my heart. I see injustice and want to correct it. I see decisions I wish I could undo. I see how quickly people can hurt one another. And sometimes I see all of this and wonder why knowing God more has not made me happier.

Then today's Gospel gives us only a few lines.

Jesus is told that His mother and brothers are outside wanting to see Him. He answers, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and act on it."

That stopped me.

He does not say His brothers and sisters are those who understand everything.

He does not say they are the ones whose lives are peaceful.

He does not say they never become angry, frightened, exhausted, confused, or hurt.

He says they hear the Word of God and act on it.

Hear it.

Act on it.

Perhaps that is different from always feeling good because of it.

And suddenly the Psalm became more important to me:

Guide me, Lord, in the way of your commands.

That is not the prayer of someone who already knows the way.

If I knew exactly where I was going, I would not need to be guided.

Maybe faith sometimes sounds less like "I understand" and more like:

I am angry, Lord. Guide me.

I feel wronged. Guide me.

I am afraid. Guide me.

I want justice. Guide me.

I don't understand why this happened. Guide me.

I don't like what some of this suffering brings out in me. Guide me.

I am tired of trying to figure everything out. Guide me.

And perhaps that is where I am today.

I cannot explain everything that has happened this year. I cannot make every wrong right. I cannot change every person. I cannot go backward and make different decisions with information I did not have then.

But I can decide what I do next.

I can hear His Word.

And I can try to act on it.

Maybe closeness to God isn't measured by how happy I feel on a particular day. Maybe sometimes it is measured by whom I continue to follow when happiness is nowhere to be found.

I want to be His sister.

I want to belong to the family Jesus described.

Not someday when all of this is resolved.

Not when I am less angry.

Not when the finances are settled.

Not when everyone finally behaves the way I think they should.

Not when I understand why any of this happened.

Today.

Like this.

Perhaps being His sister does not mean I will always feel His peace.

Perhaps it means that when I cannot see the road, when I do not understand His ways, and when I cannot find happiness in the moment, I still turn toward Him and say:

Guide me, Lord, in the way of your commands.

And then I take the next step.
opening: I thought knowing God more would make me happier. Instead, lately, it seems the more I understand, the more I see.
title: Why Am I Not Happier?
prayer: Lord, today I come to You tired, angry, confused, and still trying. I do not understand everything that has happened, and I cannot repair everything that has been lost or hurt. But I want to remain with You. When anger speaks first, guide me. When fear takes over, guide me. When I feel wronged, guide me. When I cannot see beyond what is happening today, guide me. Teach me to hear Your Word and act on it even when I do not feel peaceful or happy. I want to be Your sister, Lord—not only when following You feels easy, but here, now, in the middle of all of this. Keep me close to You and show me the next step. Amen.
theme: Suffering, spiritual darkness, anger, perseverance, and remaining faithful by hearing and acting on God’s Word even when life does not feel peaceful or happy.

body:
Yesterday at Mass, as the priest began speaking about the Gospel of the laborers in the vineyard, he pointed out something almost uncomfortable in its honesty. When we first hear this parable, many of us probably understand immediately why the workers who had labored all day were upset.

They worked longer. They endured the heat. Then those who arrived at the end of the day received the same wage.

Something inside us says, That isn't fair.

Maybe it is envy. Maybe jealousy. Maybe comparison. Maybe simply our deeply ingrained understanding that greater effort should receive greater reward.

But then the priest said something that changed the way I heard the parable: How magnificent simply to have been called to work in His vineyard.

That stayed with me.

The workers who arrived early had something the others didn't. They had spent the entire day in the vineyard. Yet instead of seeing that as a privilege, they looked at what someone else received and suddenly felt that what they had been given was not enough.

I recognize that tendency, and frankly, I am sick of it in myself.

Why isn't our first reaction happiness for the other laborer?

Why can't I simply rejoice when someone finds a wonderful job, remodels a beautiful home, receives an unexpected opportunity, or walks into work bright and cheerful despite carrying burdens I know nothing about?

Why does comparison sometimes arrive before gratitude?

I can only speak for myself. Perhaps you don't experience this. But I suspect I am not alone.

And today's other readings seem almost perfectly placed around this uncomfortable part of the Gospel.

Isaiah tells us:

“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways.”

As high as the heavens are above the earth, so are God's ways above ours.

Perhaps that is where my questioning has to begin.

I want to understand why I react the way I do. Is it pride? Insecurity? Original sin? Some human instinct toward competition and survival? Is comparison somehow our attempt to reassure ourselves that we are doing well enough?

Maybe pieces of those explanations are true.

But perhaps I don't need to understand every mechanism inside the human heart before asking God to transform mine.

Because the vineyard exposes something much simpler.

I stop looking at the Landowner and start looking at the other laborers.

I begin calculating.

How long did she work? What did he receive? Why does their life look easier? Why did that opportunity come to them? Haven't I worked hard too?

And somewhere in all that accounting, I forget something extraordinary:

I am already standing in God's vineyard.

I was called.

I was invited in.

I have been allowed to labor for Him.

And grace is already all around me.

Then Paul takes this even further in Philippians. His words are astonishing: “For to me life is Christ, and death is gain.” He admits being caught between the two. He longs to depart and be with Christ, yet understands that remaining in the flesh is necessary for the benefit of others.

In other words: there is still work in the vineyard.

That gives our time here an entirely different meaning.

Maybe the question isn't, Why does that laborer have what I don't have?

Maybe it is:

Lord, what would You have me do while I am still in Your vineyard?

That doesn't magically eliminate envy or comparison. I wish it did.

Those thoughts can still appear before I want them to. But perhaps the first thought that enters my mind doesn't have to become the place where I remain.

I can give it to God immediately.

There it is again, Lord. I am comparing. I am jealous. I am wondering why someone else received something I wanted. I don't want this. Take it.

And then perhaps I can deliberately replace it:

Thank You for what You have given them.

Again.

And again.

And again.

Until gratitude becomes stronger than comparison.

Until another person's blessing no longer feels like evidence of my deficiency.

Until I can see God's grace in another person's life without immediately asking what it says about mine.

Perhaps this is part of what it means to labor in the vineyard. We aren't only doing God's work out in the world. God is also doing His work within the laborer.

And maybe that is why I cannot completely dissect the origin of every imperfect reaction within myself.

Isaiah has already reminded me: His thoughts are higher than mine.

I don't have to know everything.

I have to trust the One who does.

And there is tremendous freedom in that.

I don't have to determine what another laborer deserves. I don't have to calculate my position beside theirs. I don't have to understand why God gives one person this and another person that.

I can simply be grateful that when the Landowner came looking for laborers, He called me too.

Whether we arrived early in the morning or in the final hour, what an extraordinary thing it is to find ourselves standing together in His vineyard.

Not competitors.

Not accountants.

Laborers.

And how glorious it is to be one
title: Why Can't I Just Be Happy for Them?
opening: Yesterday I heard a story about a group of workers. Some worked all day. Others showed up near the end. And then, incredibly, they were all paid the same amount.  My first reaction? That isn't fair.
prayer: Lord, I give You the parts of my heart that compare, envy, judge, and keep score. When another person receives something beautiful, teach me to see Your goodness rather than my lack. When my first thought is not the person I want to be, help me give it immediately to You and choose another. Replace comparison with gratitude, jealousy with joy, and resentment with generosity. I do not understand all Your ways, nor do I need to. You called me into Your vineyard. Help me remember the privilege of being here, recognize Your grace in the lives of others, and use whatever time remains to labor faithfully for You. Amen.
theme: Envy, comparison, gratitude, God's grace, trusting God's ways, and the privilege of laboring in His vineyard

title: The Seed Is Not the Finished Thing
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
My husband and I were talking the other day about something I have wondered about many times: What will our spiritual bodies actually be like?

Then today I read 1 Corinthians 15:35–37, 42–49, and Paul is talking about exactly that. He describes our natural bodies as corruptible, weak and dishonorable, but says they will be raised incorruptible, powerful and glorious. He speaks of the natural body and the spiritual body, of Adam and Christ: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man, from heaven.” And then this extraordinary promise: just as we have borne the image of the earthly one, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly one.

There is so much there. I found myself trying to imagine it. What does a spiritual body look like? What does it mean to be raised incorruptible? We know this body—the one that grows tired, becomes sick, ages, hurts and eventually dies. But Paul tells us that this is not the finished form of what God intends for us.

And then Paul uses an image that I almost passed over: a seed.

“What you sow is not brought to life unless it dies.”

A seed.

Then I went to the Gospel, Luke 8:4–15, and there was a seed again.

Jesus tells the parable of the sower. Some seed falls on the path and is taken away. Some falls on rocky ground, begins to grow and withers because it has no moisture. Some falls among thorns and is eventually choked. And some falls on good soil, grows and produces fruit a hundredfold.

At first, I couldn't quite see what these two readings had to do with one another. Paul is talking about resurrection. Jesus is talking about receiving the Word of God. They are not telling the same parable. But the image stayed with me.

The seed.

And I realized something else. When I hear Jesus describe the different places where the seed falls, I recognize myself in all of them.

There have been times when God's Word has reached me and disappeared almost as quickly as it came. There have been times when I received it eagerly but did not allow the roots to grow deeply enough. There have been times when the thorns of life—worry, resentment, disappointment, possessions, ambition, anger, distraction—grew right alongside my faith until they began choking it.

And yes, there have also been times when the soil was good.

Sometimes when I look at all of that, I cannot stand myself. Why can't I simply be the good soil? Why do I allow the rocks back in? Why do I let weeds grow around something I know is precious?

But perhaps I have been looking at the garden incorrectly.

Jesus tells us that the seed is the Word of God. We are the soil. And when He describes the good soil, He says something I think is incredibly important: those who receive the Word bear fruit through perseverance.

Perseverance.

Maybe that is the tending of the garden.

God gives the seed. We receive it. But a garden doesn't remain healthy because a seed was planted once. There is tending to be done. There are weeds to pull. There are dry places that need water. There are rocks to uncover and remove. Sometimes something needs pruning. Sometimes we discover that what we thought was gone has grown back.

Prayer. Repentance. Forgiveness. Scripture. Eucharist. Returning when we have wandered. Beginning again when we fail.

We keep tending the garden.

And perhaps the plant that emerges can become majestic—not because of our effort alone, but because perseverance keeps us tending what God's grace has planted.

Then I returned to Corinthians, and Paul's seed suddenly looked different to me.

A seed doesn't look anything like the plant it will become. Put one in your hand and there is very little about it that reveals what is hidden inside. Bury it in the ground and something even stranger happens. It disappears. Its shell breaks apart. What looked whole is seemingly destroyed before something entirely new emerges.

If we dug it up in the middle of that transformation, we might even think something had gone terribly wrong.

Perhaps that is sometimes how we look at ourselves.

We examine ourselves in the middle of becoming and wonder why we don't look like the finished creation.

We see the rocks.

We see the thorns.

We see the places where nothing seems to be growing.

And we judge the seed because it does not yet look like the flower.

But the seed is not the finished thing.

Neither are we.

Paul tells us that what is sown in weakness will be raised in power. What is sown corruptible will be raised incorruptible. We who have borne the image of the earthly one will someday bear the image of the heavenly one.

I don't know what that spiritual body will look like. Paul doesn't really tell us that. Perhaps the greater revelation is that we cannot yet comprehend what God intends to make of what has been planted.

So maybe today I don't need to look at my unfinished garden with disgust.

I need to tend it.

Pull another weed. Move another stone. Water what has become dry. Protect what is beginning to grow. Receive His Word again tomorrow, and the day after that, and the day after that.

And persevere.

Because God is not asking the seed to already be the flower.

He is asking us to remain with Him while He brings it to life.
prayer: Lord, You know every part of the soil of my heart—the fertile places and the rocky ones, the places overgrown with thorns and the places where Your Word has taken root. Help me not to despair over what is unfinished in me. Give me the perseverance to tend what You have planted, the humility to remove what chokes Your Word, and the faith to trust what I cannot yet see. When I look at myself and see only weakness, remind me that what is sown in weakness can be raised in power. Continue Your work in me until I bear not only the image of the earthly, but the image of the heavenly. Amen.
theme: Resurrection, perseverance, receiving God's Word, spiritual growth, and trusting God with the unfinished parts of ourselves

body:
This morning, before I had even gotten to today's Gospel, my husband mentioned the women who followed Jesus. Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna. He wondered about them, and I told him to look into who they were.

Then I read today's Gospel.

There they were.

I had prayed before reading, asking God to give me some insight into what He wanted me to reflect upon today. So when I saw those same women named in Luke 8:1–3, I stopped.

Perhaps today I am simply supposed to notice them.

And so, in honor of my husband, I will.

Luke tells us that Jesus traveled "from one town and village to another," preaching the good news of the Kingdom of God. The Twelve accompanied Him, but then Luke tells us that there were women with Him as well.

And he gives us their names.

Mary, called Magdalene.

Joanna.

Susanna.

There are countless people who must have encountered Jesus during His earthly ministry whose names we will never know. Yet these women are named. Why?

Mary Magdalene had been healed by Jesus. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, a steward of Herod. Susanna is named, but Scripture tells us almost nothing else about her. Luke then tells us that these women, along with many others, provided for Jesus and the disciples out of their own resources.

I find that beautiful.

They weren't simply standing somewhere in a crowd listening to Jesus.

**They were walking with Him.**

They traveled the dusty roads. They moved from village to village. They gave what they had. They helped sustain the ministry that was carrying the Gospel into the world.

And perhaps that is exactly why Luke gives us their names.

Because following Christ isn't only found in the moments that everyone sees.

Sometimes discipleship looks like providing a meal. Giving money. Opening a home. Caring for someone. Walking beside another person. Staying when leaving would be easier. Quietly making it possible for someone else to do what God has asked of them.

And then there is Susanna.

We know almost nothing about her.

No great speech of hers is preserved. We don't know the details of her life, what she sacrificed, how long she followed Jesus, or what conversations she may have had with Him.

We simply know that **she was there.**

For some reason, that touches me.

We live in a world that often measures importance by recognition. We want to know whether what we do matters, whether anyone notices, whether our lives have accomplished enough.

Yet here is a woman about whom we know almost nothing, and nearly two thousand years later we are still saying her name.

**Susanna.**

God saw her.

Maybe that is enough.

Mary, Joanna and Susanna also remind us that the people who walk with Christ do not all come from the same place. They had different histories and circumstances. Mary had experienced profound healing. Joanna apparently lived within the household and political world surrounding Herod. Susanna's story remains largely hidden.

Different women. Different lives.

The same road behind Jesus.

Maybe that is part of what God wants us to understand.

We spend so much time wondering whether we are worthy enough, holy enough, knowledgeable enough, or important enough to be useful to God.

But Jesus simply says, **follow Me.**

Bring what you have.

Bring your resources.

Bring your wounds.

Bring your abilities.

Bring the life you actually have rather than the life you think you should have had.

And walk with Him.

Yesterday I found myself thinking deeply about my past, about forgiveness and about learning to love differently. Today the Gospel feels much quieter.

Today I see people walking.

Perhaps that is what comes after asking for mercy.

We get up and follow.

We don't have to know exactly where the road will lead. We don't have to become one of the people everyone remembers. We don't have to accomplish something enormous.

Maybe faithfulness is sometimes simply continuing to walk beside Christ and offering Him whatever we have available today.

Mary did.

Joanna did.

Susanna did.

And God remembered their names.
prayer: Jesus, thank You for the people whose quiet faithfulness has carried Your love into the world.  Thank You for Mary, Joanna, Susanna, and the many others whose names we may never know.  Teach me not to measure my life by recognition, accomplishments, or the mistakes of my past.  Show me what I have today that I can offer You.  And when I do not know what else to do, give me the grace simply to keep walking with You.  May my life, whether noticed by many or known only to You, help carry Your love somewhere it is needed.  Amen.
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
title: Follow Me....
theme: Following Jesus, faithful discipleship, women in the Gospel, and serving Christ

body:
For several days now, I have been struggling. My mind keeps wandering backward—to mistakes I have made, things I have said, the person I once was, and things that simply cannot be undone.

I have always struggled somewhat with people. Trust has never come easily to me. Somewhere along the way, perhaps much earlier than I realized, I learned to protect myself by keeping a certain distance. Rejection has a way of doing that. Eventually the protection that keeps us from being hurt can also make it difficult to love freely.

Yesterday, when I read Paul's words about love in 1 Corinthians 12:31–13:13, I found myself wondering: What if I haven't loved well enough?

That question has stayed with me.

I don't mean that I don't want to love. Quite the opposite. I want the kind of love Paul describes—patient, kind, not jealous, not quick-tempered, not keeping an account of injuries. But when I honestly examine my own heart, I recognize how difficult some of those things have been for me.

So lately I have been asking Jesus for something very simple:  Give me a new love. Give me Your love, because mine is not enough.

Then today's readings seemed to answer me.

Paul tells us that he considers himself the least of the Apostles, "not fit to be called an Apostle," because he had persecuted the Church of God. Paul couldn't change what he had done. He couldn't return to his former life and erase it.

Neither can we.

But then Paul says something extraordinary:

"But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace to me has not been ineffective."

I needed those words.

My past may explain something about me, but it does not have to be the final definition of me. God's grace can still accomplish something with the person standing here today.

Then the Gospel takes us into the home of Simon the Pharisee, where a woman known as a sinner approaches Jesus. She stands behind Him weeping. Her tears fall upon His feet. She wipes them with her hair, kisses His feet and anoints them.

Simon watches all of this and judges her.

Jesus knows exactly what Simon is thinking.

Then comes a sentence that almost stops me every time I read it:

"Simon, I have something to say to you."

Imagine sitting beside Jesus and hearing Him say your name followed by those words.

Jesus tells Simon about two people who owed debts, one much greater than the other. Neither could repay what was owed, so the creditor forgave both debts. Jesus asks which person would love the creditor more.

Simon answers, "The one, I suppose, whose larger debt was forgiven."

Jesus tells him that he has judged rightly.

Then Jesus turns toward the woman and says:

"Her many sins have been forgiven; hence, she has shown great love. But the one to whom little is forgiven, loves little."

At first, those words frightened me.

I wondered whether Jesus was saying that if I have not loved enough, perhaps I have not been forgiven.

But perhaps I had it backward.

The woman isn't forgiven because she managed to produce enough love. Her love pours out because she has encountered mercy.

She knows she needs Jesus.

Simon is looking across the room at someone else's sins. The woman is at the feet of Christ with her own.

And suddenly I understood something about love.

Maybe learning to love doesn't begin by forcing ourselves to feel differently about everyone. Maybe it begins by understanding how much mercy we ourselves have received.

Love can look very ordinary.

It can mean refusing to return an injury. It can mean being slower to judge. It can mean forgiving someone even when the memory still hurts. It can mean having mercy on someone whose story we don't understand. Sometimes it may simply mean praying, "Jesus, I cannot love this person the way You ask me to. Please love them through me."

And perhaps we need to offer some of that mercy to ourselves as well.

There are things in my past that I regret. Some can be repaired; others cannot. I can confess them. I can ask forgiveness. I can make amends where possible. But I cannot travel backward and become someone else.

Neither could Paul.

Yet Paul did not spend the rest of his life introducing himself only as the man who persecuted Christians.

He said:

"By the grace of God I am what I am."

There is a difference between remembering our sins so that they lead us toward repentance and endlessly replaying them until they lead us toward despair.

One brings us to the feet of Jesus.

The other keeps us staring at ourselves.

So perhaps when those old thoughts return, the prayer doesn't need to be complicated:

Jesus, I give You what I was.
I give You what I did.
I give You the people who hurt me and the people I have hurt.
Teach me to forgive.
Teach me to receive forgiveness.
And give me enough of Your love that I can give some of it away today.

I still struggle with this. I still have moments of judgment, mistrust, resentment and fear. I don't understand where every feeling comes from, and I don't know that I need to understand everything before bringing it to Christ.

I only need to keep coming.

Because at the end of the Gospel, Jesus does not tell the woman to spend the rest of her life terrified about whether she has been forgiven enough.

He tells her:

"Your faith has saved you; go in peace."

Maybe those words are meant for more of us than we realize.

We cannot undo yesterday. But by the grace of God, yesterday does not have to determine what we do with today.

And so today I will ask again:
prayer: Jesus, give me a new love. Give me Your love. And teach me to go in peace. Amen.
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
title: not fit to be called an Apostle?

body:
I am always looking for the gifts God gives us. Some days they are easy to recognize. Today they are harder for me to see.

Today is the Memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows, and I find myself thinking about Mary and the suffering she endured. I cannot imagine the pain she must have experienced watching her Son suffer.

And yet, in a small and very human way, perhaps I can.

We know what it is to love and be unable to protect. We know disappointment, fear, rejection and loss. We know what it feels like to ask God why something must hurt so much. There are days when this world simply feels painfully heavy.

Today is one of those days for me.

But Mary reminds me that faith does not mean we will never feel this way.

She did not escape sorrow because she loved God. She walked directly through it.

She stood beneath the Cross.

She could not change what was happening. She could not take away her Son’s suffering. She could not possibly have understood everything God was accomplishing through that terrible moment.

But she remained.

Perhaps that is the gift God is showing me today.

Not the gift of having everything resolved. Not freedom from every painful thing. Not even the ability to understand why certain things happen.

Maybe today’s gift is simply the grace to remain.

To pray when I am tired.

To trust when I cannot see very far ahead.

To get up and continue when my heart would rather stop.

Mary, Mother of Sorrows, pray for me today. Teach me your perseverance. Teach me your surrender. Teach me to remain near your Son when life hurts and I cannot understand what He is doing.

I do not ask for suffering. I ask for the faith to walk through it without losing sight of Him.

And perhaps somewhere within that prayer is the freedom I am looking for—not freedom from every sorrow of this world, but freedom from allowing sorrow to separate me from God.

Today I may not feel particularly strong.

But I can remain.

I can pray.

I can take another step.

And I can trust that even here, somewhere I cannot yet see, God is still giving gifts.

Our Lady of Sorrows, pray for us.

Jesus, I trust in You.

body:
Yesterday, standing before a relic of the Holy Cross, I found myself without the right words for what I was actually looking at. I knew, of course, what it was said to represent: a physical connection to the Cross upon which Jesus Christ suffered and died. But knowing that and standing before it were two very different things.

It was a human object, something visible and tangible, fashioned from the materials of this world. And yet what it pointed toward was entirely beyond this world.

Perhaps that is part of the mystery of the Cross itself.

Today, on the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, Jesus says to Nicodemus, “No one has gone up to heaven except the one who has come down from heaven, the Son of Man.” He then recalls Moses lifting up the serpent in the desert and says, “So must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life.”

Lifted up.

Christ would be physically lifted upon a wooden Cross. But through that Cross, He would conquer death, rise again, ascend into heaven and be seated at the right hand of the Father.

Something so ordinary—wood—became the place where heaven and earth met.

Standing before the relic yesterday, that truth suddenly felt immense.

I was looking at something material that represented something I know spiritually to be true. My eyes could see an object. My mind could understand its history and meaning to a certain point. But my soul seemed to recognize that there was something much greater before me than my intellect could contain.

And strangely, there was almost a pain in recognizing its immensity.

Not a physical pain, but the ache of realizing that God is so much greater than what the human mind can comprehend. I wanted somehow to understand the fullness of what I was contemplating: Christ crucified, Christ risen, Christ ascended, Christ seated at the right hand of the Father—and Christ still fully present to us.

But I couldn't.

And perhaps I wasn't supposed to.

There came a moment when I simply accepted the limitation of my own understanding. Instead of trying to comprehend something incomprehensible, I allowed the Holy Spirit to fill that space.

Maybe that is what faith sometimes asks of us.

We spend so much time trying to understand God. We want explanations. We want certainty. We want the mysteries of suffering, death, resurrection and eternal life to fit somewhere comfortably within the boundaries of our human understanding.

But the Cross will never fit comfortably there.

The Cross is an instrument of death that became the sign of eternal life. It represents terrible suffering and yet immeasurable love. Christ is lifted upon it in apparent defeat, and that very moment becomes His victory.

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish but might have eternal life.”

Yesterday I could see the relic with my eyes. I could stand close to it. I could contemplate what it represented.

But I could not comprehend the immensity behind it.

And for once, I did not need to.

I simply cherished the moment and allowed myself to stand in the presence of a mystery greater than I could understand.

Perhaps that is one of the gifts of the Holy Cross. It reminds us that faith does not require us to comprehend everything about God. Sometimes faith simply asks us to recognize Him, to trust what we cannot fully understand, and to allow ourselves to be overwhelmed by the enormity of His love.

The Cross stands between heaven and earth, between death and eternal life, between what we can see and what we can only believe.

And Christ is there.
prayer: Praise be Jesus Christ, now and forever. Amen.
